intro: Every day you make choices. You pick what to play. You pick what to eat. Sometimes you cannot have everything, so you choose.
In this unit you will learn about needs and wants. You will learn about goods and services. You will meet workers who make things and do things for us.
By the end, you can sort needs from wants. You can tell a good from a service. You can say what you give up when you choose.
bigQuestion: How do people choose what they need and want?

timeline.t: Wake up and eat breakfast, a need
Put on warm clothes, another need
Ride the bus to school, a service
Sort pictures into needs and wants
Choose swings or tag at recess, and give one up
Eat lunch made by the school cook
Vote on one thing to buy with the class coin jar
Walk home past shops selling goods and services

words.d: something you must have to live and stay well
something nice to have that you can live without
picking one thing when you cannot have them all
not enough for everyone who wants it
a thing you can hold or touch
work someone does for you
work a person does and gets paid money for
a person who does a job

test.why: You must have food to live. It is a need.
You can live without a toy robot. It is a want.

test.q: You have one dollar. A ball and crayons each cost one dollar (example prices). You can buy…
test.why: One dollar buys only one of them. You must choose.

test.q: You pick the ball. What do you give up?
test.why: You chose the ball, so you give up the crayons.

test.q: Two swings and six children. The swings are…
test.why: There are not enough swings for all. They are scarce.
You can hold an apple. It is a good.
A doctor does work for you. It is a service.
A job is work a person gets paid to do.

test.q: A class votes 3 for a plant and 7 for a book. What do they buy?
test.why: The book got 7 votes. 7 is more than 3.
We must have needs to live and stay well.

write.prompt: You have two dollars. A snack costs one dollar and a sticker costs one dollar. A small toy costs two dollars. These are example prices. Draw or tell what you would buy. Say what you give up.
tips: Say if each thing is a need or a want

title: Wants, Needs and Choices

chapters.title: Needs and Wants
chapters.bigQuestion: How do we choose when we cannot have everything?

story.title: One Birthday Dollar
story.kicker: Maya has one dollar and sees two things she likes.
paragraphs: It is Maya's birthday. Grandpa gives her one dollar. She holds it tight. She walks to the corner store with Mom. The sun is warm.
Maya sees a red ball on the shelf. It costs one dollar. Next to it is a box of crayons. It costs one dollar too. These prices are just for our story.
Maya wants both. But she has only one dollar. She can take home one thing. The other must stay on the shelf. What will she do?
Maya thinks hard. She loves to draw. She picks the crayons. The ball stays behind. Maya smiles. She made a choice. She feels proud.
story.think: What did Maya give up when she picked the crayons? Would you pick the same?

lessons.title: Needs Keep Us Well
lessons.mainIdea: A need is something you must have to live and stay well.
reading: You wake up hungry. You eat breakfast. Food is a *need*. Your body must have food to live.
Water is a need. Clothes that keep you warm are a need. A home that keeps you safe is a need. Without them, you cannot stay well.
Ask yourself one question. Can I live and stay well without it? If the answer is no, it is a need.

words.d: something you must have to live and stay well, like food, water, clothes or a home

look.title: A Cold Morning
look.text: Look at a boy at the bus stop. Snow is falling. He wears a warm coat. He has a hat on his head. He has a cup of water in his bag.
look.prompt: Point to the things the boy needs to stay well. Why does he need them?

check.why: Your body must have water to live. Toys and stickers are nice, but you can live without them.

check.q: A home is a need. Why?
choices: It keeps you safe and warm
check.why: A home keeps you safe and warm. That helps you stay well.

check.q: What question tells you something is a need?
choices: Can I stay well without it?
check.why: If you cannot stay well without it, it is a need.

lessons.title: Wants Are Nice to Have
lessons.mainIdea: A want is something nice to have, but you can live without it.
reading: Maya likes crayons. She likes a red ball too. These are *wants*. They are nice to have.
You can live without a ball. You can stay well without crayons. So they are wants, not needs.
Wants are not bad. Wants make life fun. But needs come first. We get needs before we get wants.

words.d: something nice to have that you can live without, like a toy or a treat

look.title: The Toy Shelf
look.text: Look at a store shelf. You see a teddy bear. You see a game. You see a bag of apples at the end.
look.prompt: Which things on the shelf are wants? Which one is a need?

check.why: You can live without a video game. It is a want.
Wants are not bad. They are nice to have. Needs just come first.
You can live and stay well without candy. So it is a want.

lessons.title: Two Piles
lessons.mainIdea: We can sort things into a needs pile and a wants pile.
reading: Ms. Lee holds up pictures. One shows milk. One shows a kite. One shows shoes. One shows a toy robot.
The class makes two piles. Milk and shoes go in the needs pile. The kite and robot go in the wants pile.
Some things are tricky. Food is a need. A big ice cream sundae is a want. Talk it over with a friend.

words.d: to put things into groups that go together

look.title: Our Class Sort
look.cite: Made-up example of one class sorting 14 pictures
look.prompt: Which pile has the most pictures? How many pictures in all?

check.why: Shoes keep your feet safe. They are a need.
A kite is fun, but you can live without it. It is a want.

check.q: The class sorted 5 needs and 7 wants. How many is that?
check.why: 5 and 7 make 12.

lessons.title: Is It a Need or a Want?
lessons.mainIdea: Some things can be a need or a want, so we think it through.
reading: Clothes are a need. A plain coat keeps you warm. A shiny coat with gold buttons is more than you need.
Water is a need. A fancy drink is a want. Both are drinks. Only one is a must for your body.
So ask what the thing does for you. Does it keep you well? Or is it just extra fun to have?

words.d: something you must have to live and stay well
something nice to have that you can live without

look.title: Two Pairs of Shoes
look.text: Look at two pairs of shoes. One pair is plain and fits well. The other pair lights up and has a cartoon on it.
look.prompt: Both pairs keep feet safe. What part is a need? What part is a want?

check.why: Water keeps your body well. The other drinks are wants.
Shoes are a need. The lights are extra fun, a want.

check.q: What should you ask about a thing?
check.why: If it keeps you well, it is a need.

lessons.title: Choose One, Give One Up
lessons.mainIdea: When you cannot have both, you choose one and give the other up.
reading: Maya had one dollar. The ball cost one dollar. The crayons cost one dollar. These are example prices.
She could not buy both. She made a *choice*. She picked the crayons. She gave up the ball.
Every choice works this way. You get one thing. You give up the other one. That is part of choosing.

words.d: picking one thing when you cannot have them all
to not get something because you picked something else

look.title: Recess Time
look.text: Look at the playground. Recess is short today. You can play on the swings. Or you can play tag. There is only time for one.
look.prompt: Which one would you pick? What would you give up?

check.q: Maya picked the crayons. What did she give up?
check.why: She could not have both. She gave up the ball.

check.q: You pick swings over tag. What do you give up?
check.why: You chose swings. Tag is what you gave up.

check.q: Why do we have to choose?
check.why: We cannot have everything we want. So we choose.

lessons.title: Not Enough for All
lessons.mainIdea: Scarce means there is not enough for everyone who wants it.
reading: Ten children want the red swing. There is only one red swing. The swing is *scarce*.
Scarce means not enough for all who want it. Time can be scarce. Money can be scarce. Toys can be scarce.
When a thing is scarce, people must choose. They can take turns. They can pick something else.

words.d: not enough for everyone who wants it

look.title: Who Wants the Swings?
look.prompt: Are there enough swings? How many children must wait?

choices: Not enough for all who want it
check.why: Scarce means there is not enough for everyone who wants it.

check.q: 10 children want swings. There are 4 swings. How many must wait?
check.why: 10 take away 4 is 6.

check.q: The swing is scarce. What can the children do?
check.why: When a thing is scarce, people choose. Taking turns is a fair choice.

lessons.title: The Class Coin Jar
lessons.mainIdea: A group can vote to choose one thing to buy together.
reading: Room 4 has a jar of coins. It holds ten dollars. That is our example amount. It is all they have.
The class wants a new ball, a plant and a book. Each one costs ten dollars in our example. The jar can buy only one.
The class votes. The book gets the most votes. The class buys the book. They give up the ball and the plant.

words.d: a way for a group to choose, where each person picks one

look.title: Room 4 Votes
look.cite: Made-up example of a class vote
look.prompt: Which thing got the most votes? How many children voted?

check.why: The book got 10 votes. That is the most.
6 and 4 make 10. 10 and 10 make 20.

check.q: The class bought the book. What did they give up?
check.why: The jar could buy only one thing. They gave up the ball and the plant.

review.why: A warm coat keeps you well. It is a need.
You can live without a doll. It is a want.

choices: Picking one when you cannot have all
review.why: A choice is picking one thing when you cannot have them all.

review.q: One cookie is left. Three children want it. The cookie is…
review.why: There is not enough for all who want it. It is scarce.

review.q: You pick a book over a game. What do you give up?
review.why: You chose the book. You gave up the game.

choices: They keep us alive and well
review.why: We must have needs to live and stay well.

chapters.title: Goods and Services
chapters.bigQuestion: Who makes the things we use, and who does work for us?

story.title: A Walk Down Main Street
story.kicker: Leo and Dad look in every window on Main Street.
paragraphs: Leo and Dad walk down Main Street. First they pass the bakery. Loaves of bread sit in the window. A baker in a white hat pulls out a hot tray.
Next is the barber shop. A barber cuts a man's hair. Snip, snip, snip. The man does not take anything home. The barber did work for him.
Then they pass the shoe store. A worker puts shoes in a box. A bus stops at the corner. The driver waves at Leo. Leo waves back.
Leo says, "Everyone here is working!" Dad nods and smiles. "Some sell things you can hold. Some do work for you. They all have jobs."
story.think: Which workers on Main Street sold a thing you can hold? Which ones did work for someone?

lessons.title: What a Good Is
lessons.mainIdea: A good is a thing you can hold, like an apple, a book or shoes.
reading: Pick up an apple. You can hold it. You can take it home. An apple is a *good*. It is a thing.
A book is a good. Shoes are goods. A pencil is a good. You can touch every one of them.

words.d: a thing you can hold or touch, like an apple, a book or shoes

look.title: Your Backpack
look.text: Look inside your backpack. You see a pencil box. You see a book. You see a lunch box with a sandwich.
look.prompt: Name three goods in your backpack. How do you know they are goods?

check.why: You can hold a book. It is a good.

check.q: How can you tell something is a good?
check.why: A good is a thing you can hold or touch.
You can hold bread and take it home. It is a good.

lessons.title: People Who Make Goods
lessons.mainIdea: Some workers make goods for other people to use.
reading: The baker makes bread. A farmer grows apples. A worker in a factory makes shoes.
These people make goods. Then other people can buy the goods. They take them home and use them.

words.d: a person who does a job

look.title: Early at the Bakery
look.text: Look at the bakery before the sun comes up. The baker mixes flour and water. She shapes the dough. She bakes it in a hot oven.
look.prompt: What good does the baker make? Who will use it?

check.why: A baker makes bread, a good.

check.q: A farmer grows apples. Apples are…
check.why: You can hold an apple. It is a good.
A shoe maker makes shoes, a thing you can hold.

lessons.title: What a Service Is
lessons.mainIdea: A service is work someone does for you.
reading: The barber cuts your hair. You do not take a thing home. The barber did work for you. A haircut is a *service*.
A bus ride is a service. A doctor's visit is a service. A teacher gives a service too.

words.d: work someone does for you, like a haircut, a bus ride or a doctor's visit

look.title: At the Doctor
look.text: Look at a girl at the doctor. The doctor listens to her heart. The doctor checks her ears. The girl feels better.
look.prompt: What work did the doctor do? Is it a good or a service?

check.why: A haircut is work a barber does for you.
The driver does work for you. That is a service.

choices: No, it is work done for you
check.why: A service is work. You cannot hold it like a thing.

lessons.title: Good or Service?
lessons.mainIdea: Ask: can I hold it? If yes, it is a good. If it is work, it is a service.
reading: A pizza is a good. You can hold it. Bringing the pizza to your door is a service. Someone did work for you.
Ask one question. Can I hold it? Yes means a good. Work done for me means a service.

words.d: a thing you can hold or touch
work someone does for you

look.title: Main Street Count
look.prompt: Are there more goods shops or service shops? How many shops in all?

check.q: Bringing pizza to your door is…
check.why: Someone did work for you. That is a service.

check.q: 5 goods shops and 3 service shops. How many shops?
check.why: 5 and 3 make 8.
You can hold a shirt. It is a good.

lessons.title: Work and Pay
lessons.mainIdea: A job is work someone is paid money to do.
reading: The baker bakes bread every day. People pay her for the bread. Baking is her *job*.
A job is work you get paid for. The bus driver has a job. The barber has a job. Money from a job helps pay for needs.

words.d: work a person does and gets paid money for

look.title: Matching Workers
look.text: Look at three cards. One shows a farmer. One shows a barber. One shows a baker. Look at three more cards: bread, a haircut, apples.
look.prompt: Match each worker to what they make or do. Which ones make a good?

check.why: A job is work someone is paid to do.
A barber cuts hair. That is a service.

check.q: Money from a job can pay for…
check.why: Money from a job helps pay for needs like food and a home.

lessons.title: What a School Buys and Hires
lessons.mainIdea: A school buys goods and pays people for services.
reading: Your school buys goods. It buys books, desks and lots of paper. It buys food for lunch.
Your school pays for services too. It pays teachers to teach. It pays a cook and a bus driver. They all have jobs.

words.d: a thing you can hold or touch
work someone does for you

look.title: Walk Through the School
look.text: Look around your school. See the desks and books. See the cook in the lunchroom. See the nurse in her office.
look.prompt: Name two goods your school buys. Name two people it pays for services.

check.why: You can touch a desk. It is a good.
Teaching is work done for you. It is a service.

check.q: Which does a school pay for as a service?
check.why: The nurse does work for students. That is a service.

review.why: You can hold a shoe. It is a good.
A doctor does work for you. It is a service.
A job is work someone is paid money to do.
Bread is a thing you can hold. It is a good.

review.q: What question tells a good from a service?
review.why: If you can hold it, it is a good. If it is work done for you, it is a service.

review.q: The school pays a bus driver. The driver gives…
review.why: Driving children is work done for them. It is a service.
